Chapter 3: The Power of Learning—Literacy as a Path to Freedom.
Imagine finding hope in the middle of hardship. When everything feels stacked against you, suddenly, there’s a glimmer—a chance to learn, to read and write. For most, education is forbidden. The people in charge know all too well that knowledge can be dangerous. It makes you ask questions, dream bigger, and maybe start to imagine a life beyond what you’ve always known.
But sometimes, opportunity shows up in the most unexpected ways.
Moving to a new household brings changes, and this time, the woman's different. She isn’t used to the harsh realities of slavery, and she treats the boy with a little kindness. She even starts teaching him the basics of reading. Those first letters, the simple shapes of words—they open a whole new world. The lessons are short, but something powerful takes root. Suddenly, literacy isn’t just a skill. It’s a key—a way out, a path to freedom.
Of course, it doesn’t last. The master finds out and shuts it down fast. He’s firm: teaching an enslaved person to read is too dangerous. It’ll ruin them for servitude, he claims. The message couldn’t be clearer—knowledge is power, and they intend to keep that power locked away.
But here's the thing: once you’ve had a taste of learning, you can’t unlearn how important it is. The boy realizes—if the masters are this afraid of education, it has to matter.
Determined to keep going, he gets creative. Scraps of paper become treasures. Any chance to read, he grabs it. He even trades bread for lessons, asking neighborhood kids to help him with words and sentences. Every new word is a tiny victory—a step closer to understanding a world so much bigger than the plantation.
It isn’t easy. Sometimes it feels like two steps forward and one step back. There are plenty of moments where doubt creeps in. But the urge to learn is stronger than any setback. With each new skill, his confidence grows. He starts to see himself differently—not just as property, but as a person with thoughts, dreams, and a future of his own.
Of course, literacy doesn’t just bring hope. It also brings tough questions. Suddenly, he’s more aware of the injustice all around him—the lies used to justify slavery, the possibility that life could be different. The more he learns, the hungrier he becomes for freedom. He finds the words of abolitionists in old newspapers and worn-out books, and they light a fire inside him. They prove that others have fought this fight, and that real change is possible.
In the end, this journey toward literacy isn’t just about reading and writing—it’s about reclaiming your identity, refusing to accept the limits others try to place on you. It’s a quiet act of rebellion—a way of saying, "I am more than what you say I am."
